ethiopia.summary: Renewed fighting in Tigray, Ethiopia, has severely strained the region's already fragile healthcare system, pushing it closer to collapse. Hospitals in Mekelle have been overwhelmed by casualties from recent clashes between Ethiopian federal forces and Tigrayan fighters, which reignited a two-year cessation of hostilities. Medical staff report chaotic conditions, with emergency rooms flooded and resources stretched thin. The conflict has exacerbated existing shortages of healthcare workers, medicines, and ambulances, with many doctors going unpaid for months. The World Health Organization has warned that ongoing violence is further undermining healthcare access. Attacks on medical facilities have persisted, with reports of looting and armed takeovers, complicating the delivery of essential services. A healthcare worker noted over 100 maternal deaths in the past year due to a lack of resources. The situation reflects a deepening crisis, with the region's healthcare infrastructure still reeling from the devastating Tigray war of 2020-2022.

ethiopia.title: Tanzanian Delegation Interested in Ethiopia's Agricultural Commodity Standards Practice
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Tanzanian Delegation Interested in Ethiopia's Agricultural Commodity Standards Practice - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Tanzanian Delegation Interested in Ethiopia's Agricultural Commodity Standards Practice 10 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Tanzania's Capital Markets Tribunal Chairperson, Ntemi Nimilwa Kilekamajenga, has expressed interest in Ethiopia's experience in ensuring that agricultural commodities meet international market standards, citing the Ethiopian Commodity Exchange's quality assessment practices and specialized academy as valuable institutional lessons. The Tanzanian delegation head told ENA that the delegation was particularly impressed by the Commodity Exchange's extensive range of traded agricultural products and the academy which plays an important role in ensuring the quality of agricultural commodities destined for export. He noted that Ethiopia trades a wider range of agricultural products than Tanzania, citing maize, which is not currently among the commodities traded through Tanzania's commodity exchange, as one example. The delegation head identified the Ethiopian experience as an important lesson, particularly the need to consider expanding the range of agricultural products traded through Tanzania's commodity exchange. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Kilekamajenga said the academy established by the Ethiopian Commodity Exchange was a notable practice that a Tanzanian commodity exchange staff should visit Ethiopia and learn how the institution ensures exported agricultural products meet internationally required quality standards. He stated that Tanzania's Ministry of Finance accompanying the delegation had also developed an interest in exploring ways to facilitate such a learning visit upon their return. The delegation also gained firsthand insight into how the exchange applies its quality assurance system, particularly in assessing coffee destined for international markets, Eliad E. Mndeme, a Tanzanian lawyer and member of the delegation, said. He said the delegation was taken through the coffee assessment process, which involves evaluating its taste, aroma and preparation; and also had an opportunity to participate in testing the coffee. Mndeme said the quality assurance mechanism gives international buyers confidence that coffee traded through the exchange meets the required standards. He also highlighted the financial benefits of the system, explaining that farmers who obtain quality certificates from the exchange can use them to secure bank loans as the certificates serve as tradable. The two sides discussed ways to strengthen bilateral relations, advance cooperation on climate action and address regional issues of mutual interest. Upon his arrival in Antalya, the Prime Minister said: "I held a productive bilateral meeting with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan of Türkiye. During our discussion, I congratulated him on the preparations for hosting COP31 and the efforts underway towards its successful delivery." In a statement posted on his X account, PM Abiy said the two leaders explored opportunities to further deepen the strong partnership between their countries, including cooperation as Ethiopia prepares to assume the COP32 Presidency in 2027. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines They also exchanged views on regional developments and issues of mutual interest, reaffirming their commitment to strengthening bilateral relations and translating shared priorities into tangible progress. "Throughout our talks, we reaffirmed our shared commitment to advancing our partnership and making tangible progress on areas of common priority," the Premier noted. The meeting highlights the growing importance of Ethiopia-Türkiye cooperation as the two countries take on consecutive COP presidencies, with Türkiye hosting COP31 and Ethiopia preparing to welcome the global climate community to Addis Ababa for COP32, ENA learned. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Pledges Inclusive COP32 Process, Puts LDC Priorities At Center of Climate Agenda
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Pledges Inclusive COP32 Process, Puts LDC Priorities At Center of Climate Agenda - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Pledges Inclusive COP32 Process, Puts LDC Priorities At Center of Climate Agenda 10 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia reaffirmed its commitment to advancing the climate priorities of Least Developed Countries (LDCs), pledging an inclusive, transparent and collaborative process as it prepares to host the 32nd United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP32) in Addis Ababa in November 2027. Foreign Affairs Minister and COP32 President-Designate Gedion Timothewos reaffirmed the commitment during talks with LDC Group Chair Ambassador Adão Soares Barbosa of Timor-Leste at the Ethiopia Pavilion on the sidelines of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. Gedion underscored the importance of close consultation and strong partnerships to ensure that the priorities, interests and perspectives of LDCs remain central to COP32 preparations and deliberations. He stressed that Ethiopia intends to work closely with the LDC Group and other international partners to build consensus and advance climate outcomes that reflect the shared aspirations of vulnerable countries. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The Minister also emphasized that a successful COP31 would provide a critical foundation for COP32, helping sustain momentum in global climate negotiations and deliver meaningful progress on collective climate action. Ethiopia is using its participation in COP31 to strengthen international partnerships, support constructive negotiations and build momentum for its upcoming presidency. Speaking on Monday, Gedion said Ethiopia's foremost priority at the Antalya conference is to contribute to a successful negotiation process that will lay a strong foundation for more effective outcomes at COP32. To this end, Ethiopia will work closely with the Turkish and Australian COP31 presidencies to support ongoing negotiations and facilitate a smooth and constructive transition to the next climate conference. Mobilizing international partnerships and building a shared understanding of Ethiopia's COP32 vision are also central to the country's engagement, he said, adding that the government is seeking to exchange perspectives, identify common interests and establish areas of cooperation with potential partners. Ethiopia also aims to use the global climate gathering to generate wider international interest in COP32 and encourage broad participation in the Addis Ababa summit. Gedion noted that the Ethiopia Pavilion is serving as a platform for dialogue, partnership-building and showcasing the country's climate initiatives, while offering international participants an early glimpse of Ethiopia's preparations and hospitality as the next COP host. As Ethiopia prepares to host COP32, the country is intensifying diplomatic engagement with international partners to build cooperation, mobilize support and advance an inclusive and action-oriented global climate agenda. ethiopia.title: Reexamining Ethiopia's Ethnic Federal Model to Advance Peace and Security
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Reexamining Ethiopia's Ethnic Federal Model to Advance Peace and Security - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Reexamining Ethiopia's Ethnic Federal Model to Advance Peace and Security 10 November 2026 Africa Center for Strategic Studies (Washington, DC) By Joseph Siegle and Hany Wahila Reforming Ethiopia's ethnic federal model provides an opportunity to pivot away from the persistent instability generated by ethnic militias, though this will require opening political space as well as disarmament. Attacks launched by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies against the federal government in September 2026 raised fears of a return to the destructive conflict of 2020-2022, in which an estimated 600,000 people perished. While the federal government subsequently regained control over virtually all of the territories taken during the offensive, concerns persist that instability in northern Ethiopia could trigger a wider regional war--potentially colliding with the catastrophic conflict in Sudan and drawing in rival, well-resourced Gulf States. Overshadowed by these regional tensions are Ethiopia's ongoing domestic security challenges. The TPLF attacks were launched under the rubric of the so-called "Alliance for Survival"--comprised of a disparate coalition of seven Ethiopian armed groups: Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM) Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF) Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (ARDUF) Benishangul People's Liberation Movement (BPLM) Gumuz People's Democratic Movement (GPDM) Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Representing dissident factions from their respective regions, the stated objective of the Alliance is to overthrow the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. While loosely organized (the alliance was declared just weeks before the September attacks), each of the seven groups had taken up arms against the government over the preceding years (and in some cases decades). Some were part of a precursor alliance formed in 2006 . The Ethiopian federal government's 2023 decision to integrate all regional militias under the federal army or police following the destructive Tigray conflict has met armed resistance from these and other militias, propelling an escalation in violent clashes in recent years. Fighting involving these groups and federal forces has resulted in an average of 1,500 clashes and 4,900 battle-related fatalities annually since 2024. Roughly 90 percent of these fatalities are linked to two groups: the Amhara Fano National Movement (60 percent) and the Oromo Liberation Army (30 percent). Left to fester, the threat from regional militias poses a deeper source of instability for the country. Ethiopia's ethnic federal model represents a source of structural instability. The militias' unwillingness to disarm and accept a unitary chain of command under the federal government exposes a structural defect in Ethiopia's ethnic federal model. Established by the TPLF-led federal government in 1995, the model created ethnically based jurisdictions and gave regions the right to secede. The constitution also authorized regional police forces, which have evolved into militarized special forces . Experience from other federal systems shows that ethnically based political jurisdictions and autonomous regional security forces contribute to fragmentation and increase the likelihood of conflict . Understanding the political, economic, and security drivers of Ethiopia's regional militias, therefore, can provide context for how the country addresses these persistent domestic security challenges and how it builds a federal governance structure that can be resilient and responsive to the diverse needs of Ethiopia's 135 million citizens. Tigray Region The political-security equation in Tigray is unique given the dominant role the TPLF held in national politics for nearly three decades. When the ruling Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Defense Forces (EPRDF) dissolved in 2019, the TPLF retained considerable political influence, experienced military commanders, and military assets. The unwillingness of the TPLF leadership to accede to federal authority set the stage for the 2020-2022 conflict. Even following the TPLF's 2022 defeat and the signing of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement (COHA, also referred to as the Pretoria Agreement), hardliners in the TPLF, led by Debretsion Gebremichael, have attempted to undermine federal authority in Tigray. Debretsion was the former Minister of Communications and Information Technology and the Deputy Prime Minister in Ethiopia during EPRDF rule. Established under the COHA, the Tigray Interim Administration (TIA) was intended to facilitate the reintegration of Tigray into Ethiopia's federal structure. The TIA's authority, however, has been consistently challenged by the Debretsion-led faction of the TPLF, including the failure to give up heavy weapons as stipulated under COHA. This resistance grew more brazen over time, ultimately resulting in the TPLF unilaterally asserting the reinstatement of the pre-2022 regional council in April 2026. The majority of Tigray's citizens did not support the TPLF reigniting the conflict with the federal government. This power grab was rejected by many Tigrayans . A statement by the Salsay Weyane Tigray party in May 2026 captured these concerns: "For over three decades, this organization [the TPLF] has monopolized the politics of Tigray. It has now devolved into a tool for competing factions to seize power by force, making the gun the primary rule of the political game." This view was a recurring theme of a coalition of Tigrayan opposition parties that formed the Covenant for Radical Change in 2023, calling for political reforms in the region. TPLF hardliners were emboldened by an undeclared alliance with Eritrea that is believed to include access to weapons and deployment of Eritrean military forces in Tigray. This deepening belligerence culminated in a declaration of war and seizure of federal government assets in Tigray on September 23, 2026. Subsequent fighting with federal forces resulted in at least 277 battle-related fatalities. What becomes of the TPLF hardliners will be a central issue for the region moving forward. Given that the party has twice launched violent attacks on the federal government--at great cost in lives, economic loss, and regional stability--it has limited credibility as a democratic political actor. Rebuilding Tigray as part of Ethiopia's federal structure involves far more than the TPLF, however. Still recovering from the previous conflict, the majority of Tigray's 7.5 million citizens did not support the TPLF hardliners reigniting the conflict with the federal government. This limited support, underscored by the widespread evasion of the TPLF's forced conscription, is a key factor in the rapid collapse of the TPLF offensive in September and October 2026. The TPLF's short-lived territorial gains were also due to the creation of the Tigray Peace Force (TPF) in 2025. The TPF was formed by disaffected TPLF fighters who saw no future for themselves under the TPLF leadership and believed they should be defending Tigray rather than " preserving the same old elite ." The TPF contends that the Tigrayan military should be apolitical rather than aligned with one party. When fighting broke out in 2026, the TPF fought with the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) to repulse the TPLF offensive. Western Tigray A flashpoint in tensions between the Tigray and Amhara Regions is the status of Western Tigray (also known as Wolkayit). The jurisdiction was the focus of some of the most vicious violence during the 2020-2022 conflict, after which many Tigrayan residents were forced to flee the area and the land subsequently settled by Amhara communities. The region is the focus of competing territorial claims linked to iterative episodes of forced displacement and resettlement from previous eras. The COHA does not explicitly address the status of the area, and the federal government has called for a referendum by the territory's residents to resolve the matter. Tigrayans contend this solution would not account for the estimated 800,000 Tigrayans who have been displaced since 2020. The ongoing uncertainty and polarization around this issue have been a justification for militias in both Tigray and Amhara to retain their arms. After reclaiming the regional capital of Mekelle and other parts of Tigray, the federal authorities appointed a new TIA leadership, comprised of ethnic Tigrayans, in October. Their mandate is to oversee elections by April 2027, restore basic public services and infrastructure, and facilitate the return of displaced communities. Given the security challenges in the region, Tigrayans were unable to go to the polls during Ethiopia's general elections in June 2026. A participatory electoral process has the potential to redirect Tigrayan interests into institutionalized political channels--and undercut the rationale for violence. Some of the emerging political parties in Tigray include: Salsay Weyane Tigray Arena Tigray for Democracy and Sovereignty Tigray Democratic Solidarity National Congress of Great Tigray The varied political affiliations within Tigray underscore that the instability in the region has been largely driven by political rivalries. As in other political jurisdictions defined along ethnic boundaries , such structures provide a ready means to politicize ethnicity. Central issues will be how best to rebuild Tigray, provide basic services, facilitate the return of displaced populations, generate investment, and clarify the authorities of the regional administration. Given Tigray's location on the border with Sudan and Eritrea, security arrangements will be particularly critical. One of the sensitivities of the implementation of the COHA was that Eritrean forces never fully withdrew from some of Tigray's border districts. The extent to which this transition is perceived by Tigrayans as representative of their interests will have far-reaching implications for the stabilization of this turbulent region. Political stability, in turn, will contribute to economic reconstruction and foster stronger integration between Tigray and the much larger Ethiopian economy. Amhara Region With an estimated 33 million people, the Amhara Region is Ethiopia's second most populous and historically the most influential. Massive youth protests in the region facilitated the dissolution of the EPRDF in 2019. Animosities built up over the 30 years of TPLF control fueled Amhara's regional militias to fight alongside the ENDF during the 2020-2022 conflict. Some of these trained and experienced Amhara militias subsequently resisted the federal government's decision to dismantle all regional forces starting in April 2023. The leader of the Amhara Prosperity Party, Girma Yeshitila, was assassinated soon after the announcement . This sequence of events triggered a spike in violence between the decentralized Fano ("freedom fighter" in Amharic) militias and the regional and federal forces that has persisted across the Amhara Region ever since. Whereas the Amhara Region had been among the most stable in Ethiopia before the 2020-2022 conflict, it subsequently has faced some of the highest levels of violence, including approximately 3,500 battle-related fatalities annually since 2024. Fano's lack of a cohesive political structure has impeded a clear articulation of the militias' agenda or negotiation positions. Composed of former youth protesters, vigilantes, and special police forces, the Fano militias claim a mandate to protect the interests of ethnic Amharas . Some make more zealous demands of Amhara ethnic nationalism and territorial claims in neighboring regions, including Tigray. Still others advocate for a greater Ethiopian identity. Collectively, the Fano militias are estimated to have 15,000-20,000 fighters. Fano's lack of a cohesive political structure has impeded a clear articulation of the militias' agenda or negotiation positions. The merger of five Fano militias under the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM) in January 2026 was viewed as a step toward a more formalized Fano structure. The AFNM's subsequent decision to sign onto the "Alliance for Survival," however, may undercut the group's ability to speak for the wider spectrum of Fano militias, most of which do not fall under the AFNM. The degree of popular support for the Fano militias is unclear. Some Fano militias have attempted to undermine the electoral process by intimidating citizens who sought to participate in the electoral process. As a result, voting did not take place in 8 of Amhara Region's 130 electoral districts. The ruling Prosperity Party claimed 117 seats in the House of People's Representatives 2026 election. In 2021, the Prosperity Party garnered 114 seats. The National Movement of Amhara (NaMA) secured six seats, and the Amhara Democratic Force Movement (ADFM) took three. The remaining seats were distributed among other parties, including the Ethiopians Citizens for Social Justice (EZEMA) party. Ethno-nationalist parties like the Argoba Unity Jeberti party are also active, though did not gain any seats. Roughly 90 percent of the fatalities linked to ethnic militias are tied to the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. NaMA alleges it has faced intimidation from federal authorities and several of the Party's elected members of parliament have been detained . In 2023, the Party's most vocal critic of the government, Christian Tadele , was charged with terrorism and possession of firearms. Despite Tadele's immunity, he was held in prison for over 3 years before being released in 2026 following a pardon. Between 80 and 90 percent of the population in Amhara rely on agriculture for their livelihoods. Incentivizing and scaling up investments to improve productivity and diversify the economy will depend on greater security in the region . Oromia Region Oromia is Ethiopia's most populous region with an estimated 43 million people. It is also one of the poorest and has not historically had significant representation at the federal level despite its relative proximity to the national capital Addis Ababa. Comprising roughly equal numbers of Muslims and Christians, Oromia has also been a focal point of periodic religious tensions . The Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) was established in the 1970s as the armed wing of the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF) to advance Oromo self-determination. OLF leaders were forced into exile following a falling out with the TPLF-led transitional government in 1992, and the group was subsequently banned in 2008. Upon coming to power in 2018, Abiy signed a peace agreement with the OLF enabling its leadership to return. A faction of the OLA, however, refused to disarm , leading to a split from the OLF. While never commanding a large following, the OLA has been resilient. While never commanding a large following (the OLA is currently estimated to have 3,000 fighters), the OLA has been resilient. Following the federal government's 2023 decision to ban all armed militias, some splinter elements of the OLA did reach agreement with the regional authorities and gave up their arms. However, violence between the main OLA faction and the federal government has escalated. This has resulted in an average of roughly 1,200 annual battle-related fatalities since 2024, destabilizing parts of western Oromia where the OLA is most active. Even though it signed onto the Alliance for Survival, the OLA has yet to coordinate military operations with its alliance partners. The Oromo Prosperity Party dominates Oromia's representation in the House of People's Representatives, controlling 167 of the 178 available seats in the 2026 general elections. The remaining nine seats were won by unaffiliated opposition candidates. The two most prominent opposition parties in the region, the OLF and the Oromo Federalist Congress (OFC) party, did not gain any representation. As in 2021, the OFC did not contest the elections, lacking confidence in the fairness of the process. The OLF did campaign in the 2026 elections (after boycotting in 2021) yet failed to win a seat. The limited opposition representation has been used as a justification for the OLA's continued attacks. The OLF has faced detention, harassment, and other restrictions that have impeded its ability to campaign. In April 2024, Bate Urgessa, an OLF spokesperson, was killed by an unknown attacker in Oromia 2 months after being detained for "conspiring to incite unrest" after speaking to a foreign journalist. The limited opposition representation has been used as a justification for the OLA's continued attacks. This includes blocking key roads and raids on foreign mining operations, demanding that extractive companies ensure local community beneficiation. An attack on the $340 million Tulu Kapi gold mine operated by UK-based KEFI Gold and Copper resulted in several fatalities and the suspension of mining operations. The OLF has called for negotiated settlements to end the clashes . They have called for proposals to establish a transitional national unity government in the Region to ensure representation and constructive engagement among opposition political parties and armed groups that have gone unrecognized by the ruling party. Ogaden, Benishangul, and Afar Regions Elements of the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF) have fought for greater autonomy of the Somali Region of Ethiopia since the 1977-1978 Ogaden War between Ethiopia and Somalia. Following the signing of a peace agreement with the federal government in 2018 as part of Abiy's reconciliation process, the majority of the ONLF disavowed armed struggle and has sought to represent the Somali Region's 13 million residents through political channels. Since signing the peace accords, the main Jijiga-faction of the ONLF has had its terrorist designation removed, re-registered as a political organization, disarmed and reintegrated most of its forces, and secured representation of 20 seats in the Regional Council during the last election cycle. The ONLF, accordingly, has been among the most successful parties to return from exile and engage in the political process. However, an old guard of the ONLF led by Abdirahman Mahadi has continued to mount guerrilla attacks against the federal government and is the faction that signed onto the Alliance for Survival. Comprised of an estimated several thousand fighters, the ONLF is linked to 111 reported fatalities in 2024, but less than 20 deaths since that time. The ONLF has been among the most successful parties to return from exile and engage in the political process. Comprising an estimated 1 million inhabitants, the Benishangul Region in northwest Ethiopia on the borders of Sudan and South Sudan is among the smallest in Ethiopia. The region is noteworthy for hosting the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD). The Region has had armed groups intermittently fighting the federal government since the 1990s, claiming to represent indigenous ethnic groups. Despite various signed political settlements in 2005, 2012, and 2022, the Benishangul Peoples' Liberation Movement (BPLM) and Gumuz Peoples' Democratic Movement (GPDM) persist in their armed struggle largely from bases in Sudan's Blue Nile State, where they are reported to be supported by the Sudanese Armed Forces . Battle-related fatalities linked to these groups have increased in recent years from 10 in 2024 to 80 in 2026. The BPLM is one of the signatories to the Alliance for Survival. The Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (ARDUF), also known as Ugugumo, has engaged in armed struggle again
ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's ethnic federal model is under scrutiny as the country grapples with ongoing instability fueled by ethnic militias. Recent attacks by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) against the federal government have reignited fears of a return to the devastating conflict of 2020-2022, which resulted in approximately 600,000 deaths. The federal government's integration of regional militias into a unified force has met with resistance, leading to increased violence and fatalities, particularly involving the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. The ethnic federal model, established in 1995, has contributed to fragmentation and conflict due to its allowance for regional autonomy and armed forces. The TPLF's refusal to accept federal authority complicates efforts to stabilize Tigray, where a new interim administration faces challenges from hardliners. Addressing Ethiopia's security issues requires a comprehensive understanding of the political dynamics among its diverse ethnic groups and a commitment to reforming the federal governance structure.

Password recovery Recover your password your email A password will be e-mailed to you. borkena Ethiopian News and Opinion Home Featured Latest News Business Opinion Video Amharic Entertainment Restaurant Travel Sport Books Blog Business Listings Jobs Support Us Contact Sign in / Join Wednesday, November 11, 2026 Facebook Linkedin Telegram TikTok WhatsApp Instagram X Youtube Home Latest Ethiopia’s Deepening Human Rights and Humanitarian Crisis Latest November 10, 2026 Updated: November 10, 2026 Ethiopia’s Deepening Human Rights and Humanitarian Crisis November 10, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Congressional Conference to Spotlight Mass Killings, Religious Persecution, and the Urgent Need for International Action Ethiopia’s Deepening Human Rights and Humanitarian Crisis: Congressional Conference to Spotlight Mass Killings, Religious Persecution, and the Urgent Need for International Action File Photo / SM WASHINGTON, D.C. — November 11, 2026 A major Congressional conference scheduled for December 11, 2026, in Conference Room 2075 of the Rayburn House Office Building on Capitol Hill will bring renewed attention to Ethiopia’s worsening human rights and humanitarian crisis. The conference comes amid mounting reports of mass killings, religious persecution, widespread displacement, destruction of property, and continuing violence against innocent civilians across multiple regions of the country. At a time when Ethiopia faces escalating political instability, ethnic tensions, armed conflict, and a deepening humanitarian emergency, the conference will provide an important platform for human rights advocates, Ethiopian American community leaders, policymakers, and other concerned stakeholders to examine the deteriorating situation and call for meaningful international action. The conference will focus particularly on the suffering of civilians in the Amhara, Oromia—including Arsi and Wollega—and Benishangul-Gumuz regions. Reports of killings, abductions, attacks on religious institutions, destruction of homes, and other serious human rights violations underscore the urgent need for independent investigations, civilian protection, and accountability. Allegations of abuses involving government security forces, regional militias, and various armed groups must be examined impartially. No individual or institution should be above the law, and no civilian should become a target because of ethnicity, religion, political affiliation, or geographic identity. Ethiopia’s Humanitarian Catastrophe: Millions Displaced and Communities Devastated Ethiopia’s humanitarian emergency has reached alarming proportions. Humanitarian reporting indicated that more than 2.9 million people were internally displaced by late 2024, while more than 141,000 Ethiopian refugees were reported to be living outside the country. These figures demonstrate the enormous human cost of prolonged conflict, insecurity, and political instability. The crisis has continued to evolve in 2026, with additional displacement reported in conflict-affected communities. Since September 2026, reports of intensified violence in the Amhara region have raised further concerns, including claims of more than one million additional people displaced. These figures require independent verification, but the reported scale of suffering demands immediate attention. Behind every displacement figure is a human tragedy. Families have been separated, children have lost access to education, farmers have abandoned their land, and entire communities have been forced to flee their homes. Many displaced families struggle to obtain food, clean water, healthcare, shelter, and basic protection. Hospitals and other essential public infrastructure have reportedly been damaged or destroyed in conflict-affected areas. Medical personnel, patients, and humanitarian workers face significant obstacles in reaching vulnerable populations. The destruction of healthcare facilities, combined with food insecurity and restricted humanitarian access, has further intensified civilian suffering. The humanitarian crisis in Ethiopia deserves the same seriousness and international attention afforded to other major global emergencies. The suffering of millions of Ethiopians must not be overlooked simply because other international conflicts dominate the headlines. Government Responsibility and the Protection of Civilians The Ethiopian government has a fundamental constitutional and moral responsibility to protect the lives, safety, religious freedom, and property of all its citizens, regardless of ethnicity, religion, political affiliation, or geographic location. This responsibility includes preventing attacks against civilians, maintaining public security, protecting religious institutions, ensuring humanitarian access, investigating credible reports of human rights violations, and holding those responsible accountable through fair and independent legal proceedings. The government cannot dismiss this responsibility or shift it entirely to regional authorities and other political actors. Protecting innocent civilians is among the most fundamental obligations of any government. The international community should continue pressing Ethiopian authorities and all armed actors to fulfill their obligations and ensure that civilians are protected. Ethnic Federalism and the Erosion of National Unity One of the central issues expected to receive considerable attention at the December 11 conference is the impact of Ethiopia’s ethnic-based federal system on national unity, political stability, and the protection of fundamental human rights. Critics of ethnic federalism argue that the system has institutionalized ethnic divisions, weakened national cohesion, and contributed to a political environment in which ethnic identity increasingly influences political representation, access to security, and relations between communities. Rather than creating a genuinely inclusive political system, the framework has, according to its critics, deepened divisions and contributed to recurring cycles of political confrontation, insecurity, and violence. The consequences have been particularly devastating for civilians in Amhara and Oromia, where communities have experienced repeated attacks, displacement, and insecurity. Ethiopia needs a political and constitutional framework that guarantees equal citizenship and protects the fundamental rights of every Ethiopian. National unity must not require the suppression of cultural, linguistic, or religious diversity. Instead, diversity should be protected within a democratic system founded on equality, individual rights, constitutional guarantees, and the rule of law. The conference will provide an opportunity to discuss comprehensive constitutional reform, inclusive political dialogue, and the development of independent institutions that serve all Ethiopians equally. Mass Killings and the Persecution of Ethiopian Orthodox Christians Among the most disturbing aspects of Ethiopia’s human rights crisis are reports of continuing attacks against Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Christians, including targeted killings, attacks on places of worship, and the destruction and burning of religious institutions. Reports emerging from Arsi, Wollega, and other parts of Oromia have described horrific attacks against Orthodox Christian communities. In several reported incidents, civilians have allegedly been targeted because of their religious identity, while churches, homes, and other religious properties have been attacked or destroyed. The suffering of Ethiopian Orthodox Christians cannot be separated from the broader human rights crisis affecting the country. Religious persecution, ethnic violence, and political instability have become interconnected challenges that demand immediate attention. The Ethiopian government has a constitutional and moral obligation to protect religious freedom and ensure the safety of every religious community. The protection of churches, mosques, monasteries, clergy, worshippers, and other religious institutions must be guaranteed under the law. Repeated attacks, coupled with concerns about inadequate investigations and the absence of accountability, raise serious questions about the effectiveness of existing security and law enforcement mechanisms. The deliberate targeting of civilians because of their religious or ethnic identity must never be tolerated. The international community should take seriously credible warnings of potentially genocidal violence and support impartial investigations into allegations of mass atrocities. Religious freedom is a fundamental human right, not a privilege granted by political authorities. Transitional Justice Without Accountability Is Not Justice Another important issue is Ethiopia’s transitional justice process, which was presented as a mechanism for addressing past atrocities, promoting reconciliation, and establishing accountability. However, serious concerns remain regarding transparency, independence, inclusiveness, and the implementation of meaningful reforms. A transitional justice process cannot succeed if victims and affected communities are excluded, perpetrators remain unaccountable, or investigations are influenced by political considerations. Justice must be applied equally, regardless of ethnicity, political affiliation, religious identity, or government position. Ethiopia needs an independent and credible accountability mechanism capable of investigating serious violations committed by all parties to the conflict. Victims and survivors must have meaningful opportunities to participate in the process, and those responsible for serious crimes must face appropriate legal consequences. Without accountability, reconciliation becomes an empty promise. Sustainable peace cannot be built on impunity, selective justice, or the deliberate exclusion of affected communities. The Responsibility of the United States and the International Community The December 11 Congressional conference will also examine the important role the United States can play in encouraging a peaceful, democratic, and stable future for Ethiopia. The United States has historically maintained significant diplomatic, economic, and security relationships with Ethiopia. These relationships provide Washington with considerable diplomatic influence and opportunities to encourage respect for human rights, civilian protection, democratic governance, and political reform. Under President Donald Trump, the administration and Congress should give renewed attention to Ethiopia’s deteriorating humanitarian and security situation. Addressing this crisis should be viewed not only as a human rights priority but also as an important component of U.S. policy toward the Horn of Africa. Congressional leadership and bipartisan engagement are particularly important. Members of the House and Senate should consider stronger oversight, bipartisan legislative initiatives, targeted sanctions against individuals credibly implicated in serious human rights violations, and appropriate conditions on U.S. assistance. Such measures should be carefully designed to promote accountability without worsening the suffering of ordinary Ethiopians. The United States should also work closely with the United Nations, African Union, European Union, and regional partners to advance the following priorities: Immediate Protection of Civilians: Press the Ethiopian government and all armed actors to end attacks against civilians and protect vulnerable communities. Independent Investigations: Support credible and impartial investigations into reported mass killings, religious persecution, forced displacement, and other serious human rights violations. Expanded Humanitarian Assistance: Improve access to emergency food, medicine, shelter, and healthcare for displaced populations and communities affected by conflict. Accountability and Justice: Pursue appropriate consequences for individuals responsible for atrocities and ensure that transitional justice mechanisms are independent, transparent, and inclusive. Inclusive National Dialogue: Encourage a genuinely inclusive political process involving all major stakeholders, including representatives of Amhara, Oromo, Tigrayan, and other Ethiopian communities. Democratic and Constitutional Reform: Support fundamental freedoms, religious liberty, freedom of expression, independent media, judicial independence, and free and credible elections. Stronger International Diplomatic Engagement: Strengthen U.S. diplomatic leadership in the Horn of Africa and coordinate efforts with regional and international institutions to prevent further destabilization. The United States should use its diplomatic relationships and international partnerships to encourage a peaceful political process that addresses the underlying causes of Ethiopia’s conflicts. Ethiopia’s Crisis Is a Threat to Regional Stability Ethiopia is strategically important to the Horn of Africa and the African continent. Its continued instability carries consequences extending well beyond its national borders. The country’s conflicts and humanitarian emergency have contributed to population displacement and placed additional pressure on neighboring countries, including Sudan and Kenya. Continued instability also threatens regional security, economic development, cross-border cooperation, and the broader interests of the international community. With a population exceeding 120 million, Ethiopia is one of Africa’s most strategically significant countries. Its stability is essential not only to the well-being of its citizens but also to the long-term security and economic development of the Horn of Africa. The international community cannot afford to wait until the crisis becomes even more difficult to contain. Preventive diplomacy, inclusive political engagement, and sustained international attention are urgently needed. Ethiopian Americans Urge African Union to Include Amhara People in Ethiopia’s Peace Process The importance of an inclusive political process was also emphasized in a recent interview with Channel Africa, during which Ethiopian American civic advocates discussed their appeal to African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf. The Coalition of Ethiopian Americans Civic Organizations called on the African Union to support an inclusive and sustainable peace process that gives the Amhara people and all major stakeholders a meaningful voice in discussions concerning Ethiopia’s future. The advocates expressed concern that the Pretoria Agreement was limited to its signatories, while other conflicts, civilian suffering, displacement, and serious human rights concerns continued across Ethiopia. Their appeal to the African Union emphasized four important priorities: Inclusion of the Amhara people and all major stakeholders in peace negotiations. Protection of civilians and religious freedom. Impartial investigations and accountability for human rights violations. Meaningful national dialogue addressing the underlying causes of conflict. As emphasized during the interview, military action alone cannot deliver lasting peace. Ethiopia needs inclusive dialogue, justice, accountability, and genuine national reconciliation. Channel Africa Interview: Listen to the interview: Ethiopian Americans Call on the African Union to Ensure Amhara Inclusion in Ethiopia’s Peace Process A Call to Action: Ethiopian Americans Must Make Their Voices Heard The December 11 Congressional conference represents an important opportunity to bring the voices and concerns of suffering Ethiopians directly to policymakers in Washington. For Ethiopian Americans, this is more than a political discussion. It is a humanitarian responsibility and a commitment to defending the fundamental rights, dignity, and lives of innocent civilians in their homeland. Ethiopian Americans are taxpayers, constituents, and active members of American society. They have every right to ask their elected representatives to pay attention to the suffering of millions of people in Ethiopia and to use America’s diplomatic influence to encourage meaningful change. Community participation and sustained advocacy are essential. Ethiopian Americans should continue contacting their representatives in Congress, sharing credible reports, supporting independent human rights documentation, and encouraging bipartisan action. Accurate information is equally important. The international community cannot respond effectively without reliable reporting, independent documentation, and the willingness of human rights advocates, journalists, religious leaders, and affected communities to speak openly about atrocities. Silence and indifference risk allowing impunity to flourish and further violence to continue. Ethiopia deserves a future built on democratic governance, equal citizenship, constitutional protections, religious freedom, national reconciliation, and respect for human dignity. No ethnic group, religious community, or political constituency should be left vulnerable to violence or denied equal protection under the law. The United States Congress, the Trump administration, and the international community must recognize that protecting innocent civilians is not optional. It is a fundamental responsibility under international human rights principles. The December 11 Conference: An Opportunity for Meaningful Action The December 11 Congressional conference on Capitol Hill is an opportunity to move beyond expressions of concern and toward concrete policy recommendations and sustained international engagement. The conference seeks to elevate the experiences of victims and affected communities, encourage bipartisan Congressional attention, and advance practical measures to protect civilians, promote accountability, and support an inclusive political process. The central message is clear: Ethiopia’s human rights and humanitarian crisis must no longer be ignored. The lives and dignity of innocent Ethiopians matter. The time for meaningful international engagement, accountability, and the protection of civilian lives is now. Ethiopia needs peace, justice, democracy, and equal protection for all its citizens. The international community must act before more innocent lives are lost. Reports indicate that over 2.9 million people are internally displaced, with additional violence in regions like Amhara and Oromia exacerbating the situation. The conference will provide a platform for human rights advocates and policymakers to discuss the urgent need for international action and independent investigations into human rights violations, particularly against Ethiopian Orthodox Christians. Critics of Ethiopia's ethnic federalism argue it has deepened divisions and contributed to violence, necessitating a political framework that promotes equality and protects diversity. The Ethiopian government is urged to fulfill its constitutional duty to protect all citizens, while the international community is called upon to support accountability and civilian protection efforts. The U.S. can play a crucial role in promoting human rights and stability in Ethiopia through diplomatic engagement and legislative initiatives.

ethiopia.title: Tens of Thousands Flee Into Kenya As Clashes Erupt in Ethiopia's Moyale
ethiopia.content: Kenya: Tens of Thousands Flee Into Kenya As Clashes Erupt in Ethiopia's Moyale - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Kenya: Tens of Thousands Flee Into Kenya As Clashes Erupt in Ethiopia's Moyale 10 November 2026 Radio France Internationale By RFI Humanitarian groups in Moyale in northern Kenya are calling for urgent funding to support tens of thousands of people who have fled violent clashes in southern Ethiopia. About 50,000 people have crossed into the Kenyan side of Moyale, a border town straddling northern Kenya and southern Ethiopia , where many are struggling to find food, water and shelter. "Families who fled are facing serious shortages of food, water and adequate shelter, while the communities hosting them already have limited resources," said Nomagugu Ncube , Kenya chief of mission for the UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM). Hosts under strain Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Most of the displaced are staying with relatives or members of the local community, which puts pressure on food and water supplies that were already scarce. Others have taken refuge in schools and temporary sites, and some are sleeping outdoors. The displacement follows renewed violence linked to a long-running dispute between Ethiopia's Oromia and Somali regions over land and administrative control. On 18 October, a Somali flag was raised at an administrative office in Ethiopia's Moyale, a city jointly administered by the two regions. This triggered an exchange of gunfire between local militias in which a 13-year-old girl was killed, sparking protests and further violence. Thousands flee The fighting spread across seven districts, leaving more than a dozen people dead and forcing tens of thousands to flee, many of them across the border into Kenya . The Kenyan government is working with the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, to register new arrivals and assess their needs. Other humanitarian organisations, including the Kenya Red Cross, are also providing aid. The Kenya Red Cross initially put the number of displaced people at 36,000. The IOM has since raised its estimate to 50,000, but the figure could rise further as assessments continue, and no comprehensive official count is yet available. Approximately 50,000 individuals have crossed the border, facing severe shortages of food, water, and shelter. Many displaced families are staying with local relatives, putting additional strain on already limited resources. Others have sought refuge in schools or temporary sites, with some sleeping outdoors. The violence escalated after a Somali flag was raised in Moyale, leading to gunfire between local militias and resulting in multiple fatalities, including a 13-year-old girl. As assessments continue, the number of displaced individuals may rise further.

somalia.content: Somalia, Türkiye discuss security cooperation and counterterrorism efforts - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY Somalia, Türkiye discuss security cooperation and counterterrorism efforts Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Wednesday November 11, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia and Türkiye discussed military and security developments, counterterrorism operations and bilateral security cooperation during talks in Mogadishu, as the two countries seek to deepen a longstanding defense partnership. Türkiye’s ambassador to Somalia, Ferhat Alkan, met National Security Adviser Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed on Tuesday for talks focused on Somalia’s security situation and efforts against al-Shabab, according to statements from the Turkish Embassy and Somali officials. The meeting also covered political developments and broader security coordination between Ankara and Mogadishu. advertisements “Türkiye remains committed to contributing to Somalia’s peace, stability and security, as it has done in the past and continues to do today,” the Turkish Embassy said. Somalia’s National Security Adviser expressed appreciation for Türkiye’s longstanding support and stressed the importance of continued coordination between the two governments, according to Anadolu Agency. The talks come as Somalia continues military operations against al-Shabab while also navigating changes in the international security presence supporting the country. Türkiye is one of Somalia’s closest security partners and operates the TURKSOM military training facility in Mogadishu, which has trained thousands of Somali soldiers and officers. Turkish support has included military training, logistical assistance and institution-building for Somalia’s armed forces. Alkan also met Somali Defense Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi this week, with discussions focused on strengthening defense cooperation, building the capacity of the Somali National Armed Forces and reviewing regional security developments. The Somali government has described Türkiye as a strategic partner in its efforts to strengthen national security institutions and reduce reliance on foreign forces. Alkan assumed his post as Türkiye’s ambassador to Somalia on Sept. 21, succeeding Alper Aktaş. somalia.content: AUSSOM chief, Swedish ambassador discuss Somalia security and international support - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY AUSSOM chief, Swedish ambassador discuss Somalia security and international support Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Wednesday November 11, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — The head of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) met Sweden’s ambassador to Somalia on Monday to discuss the country’s security situation, implementation of the mission’s mandate and continued international support for peace and stabilization efforts. Amb. El Hadji Ibrahima Diene, the special representative of the African Union Commission chairperson SRCC and Head of AUSSOM, met Swedish Ambassador Hans Lundquist in Mogadishu, according to the mission. The two officials reviewed recent developments in Somalia and discussed cooperation between AUSSOM, the Federal Government and international partners. advertisements Diene praised Sweden’s longstanding engagement with Somalia and the African Union, including support for peacebuilding and stabilization. Lundquist reaffirmed Sweden’s commitment to working with the Somali government, AUSSOM and international partners to advance sustainable peace and stability. Sweden has maintained development and humanitarian engagement with Somalia for decades. Its current cooperation strategy for 2026-2028 includes support for state-building, democratic governance, human rights, resilience and economic opportunities. AUSSOM, which replaced the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia in January 2025, is mandated to support Somali security forces, help degrade al-Shabab, protect key population centers and infrastructure, and assist Somalia’s broader security transition. Diene currently heads the mission as the African Union Commission chairperson’s special representative for Somalia. The meeting comes as AUSSOM continues to rely heavily on international financial and political support while Somalia gradually assumes greater responsibility for national security. somalia.content: Cruz Ties Somalia Ambassador Nominee's Confirmation to Somaliland News Rankings Platform Federal State Elections Pro Pricing Sign In Sign Up Free Advertisement Cruz Ties Somalia Ambassador Nominee's Confirmation to Somaliland By Legis1 Editorial · Edited by Carolyn Robinson Wednesday, November 11, 2026 · 1 min read Why it Matters The Senate Foreign Relations Committee held a hearing on Nov. 10 for 10 State Department nominees. The committee, chaired by Sen. Jim Risch (R-ID) , heard nominees for ambassadorships including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Somalia and Ecuador, plus the ambassador at large for international religious freedom. ​ What They're Saying During the discussions, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) told State Department nominee Devin Kennington that his confirmation for ambassador to Somalia "depends on the State Department following the President's guidance" on Somaliland. Cruz asked Kennington what obstacles block U.S. recognition of Somaliland. Kennington said current policy recognizes Somalia's sovereignty and territorial integrity, "which includes the region of Somaliland." Pressed again, he said "I'm not in a position to answer that."Cruz responded: "I think the State Department should follow the President's guidance." Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH) questioned Wesley Hunt, nominee for Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, Department of State, on his past remarks about Islam that have been criticized by civil rights groups. Hunt said "there certainly is a faction to where that is absolutely correct," and added, "I think I was actually condemning the extremist." Sen. Tim Kaine (D-VA) pressed Jane Lynch, nominee for Ambassador at Large for International Religious Freedom, Department of State, on LGBTQ protections. Lynch said "I would never be able to support something where it's criminalizing people" over sexual identity. Shaheen told Lynch "there has not been a report produced in the last two years" of this administration, in a discussion of the overdue International Religious Freedom reports. The Bottom Line Republicans want confirmations before January, when Democrats could slow or reject controversial nominees in the next Congress. No committee vote or follow-up hearing has been scheduled to date, and committee consideration of the 10 nominations remains pending. Business Insider Edition United States International Deutschland & Österreich España Japan México Nederland Polska ADVERTISEMENT BI Africa > local > markets As Israel advances embassy plans in a breakaway nation despite warnings from China and other global powers, the US reveals why it left a key airbase in Somalia after 14 years Chinedu Okafor 11 November 2026 04:00 PM The United States (US) has revealed why, after 14 years, it decided to vacate a key airbase in Somalia, which it had occupied until a few weeks ago. Soldiers with the New Jersey Army National Guard set up an 81 mm mortar in support of a patrol at Baledogle Military Airfield, Somalia, June 24, 2019 (London Nagai/U.S. Army) The US vacated Baledogle Military Airfield in Somalia after 14 years due to the deteriorating runway, which became too costly to repair. US Army Lt. Gen. John Brennan stated the departure was an economic decision, not a sign of reduced US support for Somalia. Despite tensions over Israel's recognition of Somaliland, US-Somalia collaboration, especially in counter-terrorism against Al-Shabaab, remains strong. The airfield, crucial for intelligence gathering and training Somali soldiers, is now controlled by Ugandan and Somali troops. Army Lt. Gen. John Brennan, AFRICOM’s deputy commander, on Tuesday, noted that the US’s exit from the Somalian airfield resulted from the cost of fixing the runway. “The relocation from Baledogle was 100% an economic decision,” Brennan said during a briefing with reporters. ADVERTISEMENT “The surface of the airfield was declining to the point where it was becoming dangerous to land aircraft there,” he added. Rather than fix the runway, which was estimated to cost tens of millions, the command at the airfield decided to relocate the U.S. personnel there to Mogadishu. General noted that the departure of US troops from the airbase, as previously reported did not signal a decline of US support for Somalia, as seen on Stars and Stripes. According to him, the US’s and Somalia relationship has been growing stronger in recent months. ADVERTISEMENT The budding relationship between the two countries has recently been evidenced by a debacle between global superpowers such as Turkey, China, Saudi Arabia, and Israel concerning the recognition of Somaliland. A girl participates in a street parade in Hargeisa to celebrate Somaliland's self-declared independence. (Council on Foreign Relations) Pulse Live Kenya Complex relationship between Israel, Somalia, Somaliland and the US The cooperation between the US, which regularly partners with Somalia to conduct joint counter-terrorism airstrikes against Al-Shabaab insurgents, has taken no hit despite the actions of America's key ally, Israel, in recognizing Somaliland as a sovereign state. Somaliland and Somalia have been at odds with each other, considering that Somaliland is a breakaway state of Somalia. ADVERTISEMENT Several powerful nations have been reluctant to recognize Somaliland as a sovereign nation, except for a few, including Israel, which recently advanced plans to establish an embassy in the breakaway country , despite opposition from China, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkey, and, of course, Somalia. On November 1, 2026, Israel's Foreign Ministry confirmed that its first ambassador to Somaliland, Michael Lotem, had presented his credentials to the President of Somaliland, Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, in Hargeisa, the territory's capital, where officials also laid the cornerstone for the planned embassy. The move follows Israel's recognition of Somaliland on December 26, 2025, making it the first United Nations member state to recognise the territory since it declared independence from Somalia in 1991. Plans for the embassy have been underway for months, with Israel appointing Lotem, its former ambassador to Kenya, as its first envoy to Somaliland in April 2026. It goes without saying that Somalia has rejected this development, despite the fact that it shares a relationship with the US , a key ally of Israel. ADVERTISEMENT Even with the growing tension between Israel and Somalia, the East African country’s counter-terrorism collaboration with Washington remains active, as demonstrated when the U.S. military teamed up with the Federal Government of Somalia to execute targeted precision airstrikes against Al-Shabaab fighters near Bulo Bashiir. US Somalia stimson.org US exit of Baledogie Somali airbase Earlier this month, it was reported that military personnel from the United States (US) have withdrawn from an air base in Somalia, according to a few sources familiar with the development. The sources revealed that all U.S. personnel left the Baledogle Military Airfield, an airfield that has been central to intelligence gathering in an overarching mission to train Somalian soldiers in countering insurgent groups. ADVERTISEMENT Purportedly, the airfield is now under the control of Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) and Somali National Army (SNA) troops, one of the sources said. “In the interest of maintaining operational security, we do not discuss details of ongoing operations,” an AFRICOM spokesman said, adding that the command “repositions its forces to optimize for ongoing counterterror operations.” The United States has used Baledogle Military Airfield since 2012 to train Somalia's elite Danab commando forces and support intelligence operations, according to sources within the Somali military. somalia.content: Somalia's Statistics Bureau Becomes First Institution to Receive Swiss Funds Through Government Treasury - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Politics Nationwide Somalia’s Statistics Bureau Becomes First Institution to Receive Swiss Funds Through Government Treasury November 11, 2026 7 min read MOGADISHU , Somalia’s National Bureau of Statistics received a delegation from the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation at its headquarters in Mogadishu this week, reviewing a pilot project that is being implemented through Somali government systems rather than through parallel donor structures, a first for the agency. The delegation was led by Odile Robert, Head of International Cooperation, and Julien Peissard, Deputy Regional Director for International Cooperation for the Horn of Africa. Discussions focused on the bureau’s institutional progress, ongoing statistical programmes, and areas of cooperation under the partnership between the two institutions. According to a statement from the statistics bureau, the meeting reviewed progress under the Pilot Project on Strengthening National Statistical Capacity, which is implemented by the bureau with Swiss support. The research component, undertaken in partnership with three Somali universities, has reached the stage where finalized papers have been submitted and are currently under review. The next steps include a workshop to present findings, followed by a final dissemination workshop. A Modality That Matters The most significant detail in the statement is not the research or the surveys. It is the funding mechanism. The pilot project is being implemented through Somalia’s country systems, with project funds channelled through the Federal Government Treasury. The statistics bureau is the first national institution to implement a Swiss-supported project under this modality. This is a departure from the standard practice in Somalia, where donors have historically preferred to channel funds through international organizations, contractors, and parallel implementation units rather than through government systems. The reasons for that preference are well documented: weak public financial management, corruption risks, and limited institutional capacity. But the consequence has been that Somali institutions have been bypassed, and the capacity that donors say they want to build has not been built. The pilot project is a test of whether that can change. By channelling funds through the Treasury, the Swiss agency is placing a degree of trust in Somalia’s public financial management systems that most donors have been unwilling to extend. The risk is real. If the funds are mismanaged, the experiment will be cited as evidence that the sceptics were right. But if it succeeds, it provides a model that other donors could follow, and a pathway toward the kind of direct budget support that Somalia has long sought. The Treasury Single Account is central to that model. The Auditor General has repeatedly pushed for all government revenue to be channelled through the TSA rather than held in commercial accounts, as the Auditor General’s call for strict controls on passport revenue demonstrated . The Swiss pilot depends on the same architecture: if funds are to flow through government systems, those systems must be able to track, account for, and audit them. Statistical Modernization and Its Limits The statement also described the bureau’s efforts to modernize statistical production, including the application of satellite imagery, artificial intelligence, and geospatial analysis, alongside conventional work on the Consumer Price Index and macroeconomic statistics. These are not trivial technical matters. In a country where data has historically been scarce, contested, or dependent on international estimates, the ability to produce reliable official statistics is a marker of state capacity. The use of satellite imagery and geospatial analysis is particularly relevant for Somalia, where insecurity and access constraints make traditional household surveys difficult in large parts of the country. The bureau has been building this capacity through partnerships, including work with UNFPA on preparations for Somalia’s first population and housing census in over five decades, which relies on geospatial technology and a large-scale household survey. The bureau has also invested in how data is communicated and used. A training programme with the European Commission and the African Union Institute for Statistics focused on improving data communication capacity , recognizing that statistics are only useful if they are understood and acted upon by policymakers and the public. The bureau has presented its work at international forums, including the Global Forum on Refugee and IDP Statistics , where it showcased Somalia’s approach to integrating displacement data into official statistics. But the capacity to produce statistics is only useful if the statistics are used. The statement mentions market monitoring and the use of market-related data, but it does not describe how the data feeds into government decisions, budget allocations, or policy planning. That is the harder question. Many developing countries produce statistics that are technically sound but politically ignored. Somalia’s challenge is not only to generate data, but to create a political culture in which data shapes decisions, a challenge that extends from the first National Economic Survey to the routine work of market monitoring. The Broader Donor Context The Swiss partnership comes at a moment when donor engagement with Somalia’s institutions is under strain. As the UN political mission has closed and transferred responsibilities to Somali institutions without the accompanying budgets, and as the security transition leaves the Somali National Army with growing responsibilities and shrinking support, the question of whether donors are willing to fund Somali systems directly has become central to the country’s future. The statistics bureau’s pilot is a small test of that question. It is not a large-scale budget support programme. It is a pilot project, implemented through the Treasury, with a research component and a dissemination plan. But the principle it establishes, that Somali institutions can manage donor funds through their own systems, is significant. Other donors are watching. If the pilot succeeds, it could provide a template for other agencies that want to move away from parallel implementation but have been deterred by fiduciary risk. If it fails, the case for direct funding will be weakened, and the parallel structures that have characterized aid delivery in Somalia will be reinforced. Critical Note The Swiss Agency’s decision to fund a project through Somalia’s Treasury is a modest but meaningful step. It recognises that capacity is built by doing, not by outsourcing. If Somali institutions are never trusted to manage funds, they will never develop the systems and skills to do so. The pilot is a bet on that logic. But it is a bet, and it carries risks. Somalia’s public financial management systems have improved in recent years, but they remain fragile. The Treasury’s capacity to track and account for donor funds is not the same as the capacity of a well-established finance ministry. The audit and oversight mechanisms that donors rely on are not fully developed. The experiment could fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the statistics bureau’s competence. The broader question is whether the pilot will remain an isolated example or become a model. The statistics bureau is one institution, and its project is small. The larger challenge is whether the donors who have funded Somalia’s development for decades are prepared to move from parallel delivery to direct support at scale. The Swiss project suggests that at least one donor is willing to test the waters. The test will be whether others follow, and whether the Somali government can demonstrate that the trust being extended is justified. This pilot project, supported by the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, aims to strengthen national statistical capacity and is implemented through Somalia's public financial management systems rather than through parallel donor structures. The initiative reflects a growing trust in Somalia's financial management capabilities, which have historically been bypassed due to concerns over corruption and inefficiency.
